title: Language, Civilisation & Task Fusion — Arabic–Persian–English planned public brief

scope.goal: Plan a source-faithful public explanation of how Arabic–Persian language contact and script sharing demonstrate the difference between language, script, register, institutional history, and model processing.
scope.deliverable: A public English brief retaining Arabic and Persian source terms, an inspectable terminology table, a Unicode/script audit, visible translation losses, and unresolved disagreement.
scope.audience: General KINGDOM readers and future agents designing multilingual research, translation, verification, or localization tasks.
scope.intended_use: An inert, inspectable example of phase-separated multilingual task design over attributed public artifacts.
scope.excluded_use: Automatic routing, model execution, hidden-reasoning collection, person or culture scoring, native-speaker simulation, legal or religious authority, identity inference, publication, deployment, or proof of translation fidelity.

sources.title: The Origins of Writing as a Problem of Historical Epistemology
sources.claim_scope: Epistemic limits, inventory, and administrative concentration in early written corpora of Mesopotamia and neighbouring systems.
limitations: A specialist synthesis of fragmentary evidence, not a complete account of oral language or all early writing.

sources.title: Digital Corpus of Cuneiform Lexical Texts — Introduction to Lexical Lists
sources.claim_scope: The pedagogical and bilingual role of lexical lists in Mesopotamian scribal traditions.
limitations: Catalogue coverage reflects surviving and edited tablets rather than the full scribal ecology.

sources.title: UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology — Writing Systems
sources.claim_scope: Logo-phonetic structure and classifiers in ancient Egyptian writing.
limitations: A modern scholarly account; it cannot recover every historical pronunciation or reader practice.

sources.title: How Egyptian hieroglyphs were decoded — timeline
sources.claim_scope: Hieroglyphic, hieratic, Demotic, Greek, and Coptic script history and the Rosetta decree's multilingual setting.
limitations: A museum overview rather than a comprehensive grammatical or social history.

sources.title: Unicode 17.0 Core Specification — South and Central Asia-I
sources.claim_scope: Encoding structure, orthographic syllables, and character behaviour in Brahmi-derived scripts.
limitations: Encoding rules do not constitute a complete linguistic, paleographic, or community history.

sources.title: University of Oxford — Prakrit
sources.claim_scope: Prakrit literary and linguistic plurality alongside Sanskrit.
limitations: A concise disciplinary overview rather than a survey of every Middle Indo-Aryan variety.

sources.title: UNESCO Memory of the World — Chinese Oracle-Bone Inscriptions
sources.claim_scope: The date, royal-divinatory setting, and linguistic value of the late Shang oracle-bone corpus.
limitations: The nominated corpus is socially and materially selective and cannot represent all Shang speech or writing.

sources.title: Unicode Standard Annex #38 — Unicode Han Database
sources.claim_scope: Abstract Han character identity, properties, sources, and regional glyph considerations.
limitations: Character encoding does not determine a historical reading, language, pronunciation, or interpretation.

sources.title: Unicode 17.0 Core Specification — Europe-I: Modern and Liturgical Scripts
sources.claim_scope: The historical and typographic scope of Latin and related European script encoding.
limitations: The standard encodes text; it does not rank scripts or explain their political spread.

sources.title: Spoken Latin in the Late Middle Ages and Renaissance Revisited
sources.claim_scope: Latin use in medieval and Renaissance public documents, Roman Church administration, scholarship, schools, universities, writing, and bounded spoken settings.
limitations: The study stresses regional and social variation; Latin institutional use did not represent the everyday speech of most people or every European setting.

sources.title: Reconstructing a Prehistoric Writing System
sources.claim_scope: Linear B as the writing system used for the oldest attested written Greek dialect, Mycenaean Greek, and the methodological reconstruction linking attestations, orthography, phonetic rendering, and historical context.
limitations: A handbook chapter on reconstruction does not settle every chronology, reading, social practice, or later alphabetic development in Greek writing.

sources.title: Unicode 17.0 Core Specification — Middle East-I: Modern and Liturgical Scripts
sources.claim_scope: Arabic-script directionality, joining, contextual glyphs, and use across multiple languages.
limitations: Encoding and rendering rules do not establish language identity, reading, register, or translation.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica — Early New Persian
sources.claim_scope: Gradual development, regional setting, and transregional expansion of New Persian written in Arabic script.
limitations: Surviving written evidence does not fully disclose spoken practice or every regional variety.

sources.title: Arabic
sources.claim_scope: Arabic phonology, root-pattern and non-root-pattern morphology, inflection, and lexical structure.
limitations: A language survey cannot represent every historical or regional Arabic variety and does not make morphology a cognitive essence.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica — Arabic Elements in Persian
sources.claim_scope: Arabic lexical, orthographic, and learned-register influence within Persian.
limitations: Borrowing estimates depend on corpus, period, register, and dictionary method and do not define genealogy.

sources.title: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy — Greek Sources in Arabic and Islamic Philosophy
sources.claim_scope: Greek-to-Syriac scholarly transmission, Christian Syriac participation, translations into Arabic, continued Syriac translation, and the early Abbasid translation setting.
limitations: The entry is a scoped history of philosophical sources and records scholarly disagreement; it is not a complete history of every language, discipline, translator, or patronage network.

sources.title: The Graeco-Arabic Translation Movement
sources.claim_scope: A translation-studies account of medieval Arabic translation as meaning-remaking that combines source meaning with target knowledge rather than simple lexical equivalence.
limitations: This is one interpretive translation-studies account; its framework is not a universal theorem about all Graeco-Arabic translations or every translator.

sources.title: Centre for the Study of Manuscript Cultures — Swahili Manuscripts in Arabic Script
sources.claim_scope: Swahili Ajami manuscript practice and the effects of colonial script and language policy.
limitations: One research collection cannot represent the complete East African manuscript ecology.

sources.title: Traces of Clay: Exploring Slave and Migrant Identities in Medieval Swahili Zanzibar
sources.claim_scope: Kiswahili as a Bantu language developed on the East African coast, with medieval settlements embedded in African and Indian Ocean movement and exchange.
limitations: The archaeological argument is place-, period-, and evidence-bound and cannot define all Swahili language, ancestry, identity, or community history.

sources.title: The Historic Town and Archaeological Site of Gedi
sources.claim_scope: Gedi as a tenth- to seventeenth-century Swahili settlement within East African, Arabian Sea, Indian Ocean, Persian, Indian, and Southern Asian exchange networks.
limitations: A World Heritage property description establishes a bounded site history, not the genealogy, grammar, or full geographic history of Swahili.

sources.title: Geographic and Demographic Spread of Swahili
sources.claim_scope: Swahili spread through trade, religion, education, war, urbanization, and contact with multiple coastal, inland, and transoceanic communities.
limitations: A handbook synthesis does not make one contact process, standard variety, or demographic count an essence, value, or capability score.

sources.title: Unicode 17.0 Core Specification — Africa
sources.claim_scope: Encoding histories and structures for Ethiopic, Vai, Bamum, N'Ko, Adlam, and other African scripts.
limitations: Encoding status is not cultural vitality, historical centrality, or community consent.

sources.title: Introduction to Maya Hieroglyphs
sources.claim_scope: Logosyllabic Maya writing, sign functions, decipherment, and source media.
limitations: A teaching handbook cannot exhaust regional, temporal, or undeciphered variation.

sources.title: Library of Congress — Popol Vuh transcription and Spanish translation
sources.claim_scope: K'iche' source, Latin-script transcription, Spanish translation, oral presentation, and manuscript provenance layers.
limitations: The surviving manuscript and catalogue descriptions do not recover every earlier performance or codical witness.

sources.title: Unicode Standard Annex #29 — Unicode Text Segmentation
sources.claim_scope: Extended grapheme clusters as default, canonically stable approximations of user-perceived characters.
limitations: Default clusters may need script- or language-specific tailoring and are not universal linguistic characters.

sources.title: Unicode Standard Annex #15 — Unicode Normalization Forms
sources.claim_scope: Canonical and compatibility equivalence and normalization forms.
limitations: Normalization can preserve canonical equivalence while still losing witness-specific byte, glyph, or compatibility distinctions.

sources.title: Do All Languages Cost the Same? Tokenization in the Era of Commercial Language Models
sources.claim_scope: Model-dependent token count, price, and utility disparities across 22 typologically diverse languages.
limitations: Results are bound to the tested models, APIs, prices, benchmarks, languages, and observation period.

sources.title: SIB-200: A Simple, Inclusive, and Big Evaluation Dataset for Topic Classification in 200+ Languages and Dialects
sources.claim_scope: Topic-classification performance gaps across 205 languages and dialects.
limitations: One translated classification benchmark does not measure every language capability or cultural task.

sources.title: When Is Multilinguality a Curse? Language Modeling for 250 High- and Low-Resource Languages
sources.claim_scope: Controlled effects of data amount, language similarity, and model capacity across more than 10,000 small language models.
limitations: Models were at most 45 million parameters; results do not automatically transfer to every contemporary LLM.

sources.title: The Geometry of Multilingual Language Model Representations
sources.claim_scope: Language-sensitive means and shared mean-centred subspace structure in XLM-R across 88 languages.
limitations: The result is architecture-, layer-, prompt-, estimator-, and task-bound and does not prove a universal interlingua.

sources.title: Attention is not Explanation
sources.claim_scope: Counterexamples to interpreting ordinary attention weights as feature-importance explanations.
limitations: The experiments cover selected architectures and tasks and do not establish that attention is never causally useful.

sources.title: Is Translation All You Need? A Study on Solving Multilingual Tasks with Large Language Models
sources.claim_scope: Task- and model-dependent tradeoffs between translation to English and native-language prompting.
limitations: Results apply to the tested models, tasks, languages, prompts, and evaluation design.

sources.title: Multilingual Large Language Models Are Not (Yet) Code-Switchers
sources.claim_scope: Sentiment, translation, summarization, and language-identification evaluation on code-switched inputs.
limitations: The result is bounded to selected models, datasets, language pairs, and 2023 prompting methods.

sources.title: Prompting Multilingual Large Language Models to Generate Code-Mixed Texts: The Case of South East Asian Languages
sources.claim_scope: Prompt- and language-pair-dependent code-mixed generation across seven Southeast Asian languages or varieties.
limitations: Generation judgments and models are time- and dataset-bound; code-mixing practices are community-specific.

sources.title: United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples — implementation text
sources.claim_scope: Rights to revitalize, use, develop, and transmit languages, oral traditions, writing systems, literatures, and names.
limitations: This record does not perform legal interpretation or determine a community's consent for a particular use.

sources.title: Language Vitality and Endangerment
sources.claim_scope: A multidimensional language-vitality framework beyond speaker count alone.
limitations: Vitality factors remain contextual and cannot be converted into a culture or person score.

sources.title: KINGDOM Task Packet v1
sources.claim_scope: Existing bounded intent, criteria, authority, verification, and handoff contract.
limitations: A language weave does not itself authorize or instantiate Task Packets.

sources.title: KINGDOM Semantic Transition v0.1
sources.claim_scope: Existing structural receipts for translation, lexicalization, inference, loss, assumptions, evidence, and repair.
limitations: Receipt validity does not prove truth, fidelity, identity, intent, understanding, authority, or consent.

sources.title: KINGDOM Relational Inference v0.1
sources.claim_scope: Existing multi-probe structure, dependency, competing-model, disagreement, and non-grant contract.
limitations: Its runtime does not verify prose, evidence destinations, independence, truth, or private state.

historical_witnesses.ecology: Mesopotamian administrative and scribal contact ecology
historical_witnesses.period: Late fourth millennium BCE through later Sumerian–Akkadian scribal traditions
language_varieties: Other languages later written in cuneiform
established: Early corpora are heavily administrative.
Cuneiform later represented structurally different languages.
Lexical lists supported scribal transmission.
contested_or_missing: Everyday oral language is severely underrepresented.
Rare signs and fragmentary corpora leave readings and functions unresolved.
task_lessons: A compact institutional schema is not a universal language model.
Porting a script requires reanalysis of sign values and grammar.

historical_witnesses.ecology: Egyptian monumental, cursive, administrative, and alphabetic ecology
historical_witnesses.period: From early dynastic writing through Coptic and the last hieroglyphic inscriptions
places: Egyptian temples, administrations, and manuscript settings
established: Egyptian writing mixed phonetic and semantic functions.
Several scripts served differentiated media and audiences.
The Rosetta decree used three scripts for two languages.
contested_or_missing: Many historical vowel values and reader practices are unrecoverable.
Surviving official and sacred artifacts select social experience.
task_lessons: Record script, medium, register, and audience separately.
Multiple scripts need not mean multiple languages.

historical_witnesses.ecology: South Asian plural-script and language-strata ecology
historical_witnesses.period: At least the third century BCE through later Brahmi-descended and learned traditions
places: Regions using Brahmi and Kharoshthi inscriptions and descendants
language_varieties: Dravidian and other languages written in Brahmi descendants
scripts: Brahmi-derived scripts including Devanagari and Tamil
established: Brahmi-derived scripts use complex orthographic-syllable organization.
Prakrit names a plural and literary history rather than defective Sanskrit.
Several language families use related scripts.
contested_or_missing: Brahmi's exact genealogy and development remain debated.
Ancient everyday multilingual practice is incompletely archived.
task_lessons: Prestige labels are not quality scores or capability evidence.

historical_witnesses.ecology: Sinitic and Han character, reading, and register ecology
historical_witnesses.period: Late Shang secure corpus through modern regional character and reading systems
language_varieties: Chinese, Japanese, Korean, and Vietnamese historical character traditions
scripts: Han characters and regional glyph forms
established: The secure early corpus is royal and divinatory.
Abstract character identity does not fix one glyph or reading.
Han characters have served multiple languages and periods.
contested_or_missing: Early corpus survival strongly biases social coverage.
A code point cannot recover period, locale, pronunciation, or interpretation.
task_lessons: Bind character data to language, locale, period, and reading.
Character continuity can conceal spoken divergence.

historical_witnesses.ecology: Greek, Latin, and European script-institution ecology
historical_witnesses.period: Bronze Age Greek records through alphabetic, medieval and Renaissance institutional, print, and digital traditions
places: Regions whose languages use or adapt Latin script
language_varieties: Romance and many other Latin-script languages
established: Modern Latin script reflects medieval scribal and early Renaissance typographic transformations.
Latin continued in public documents, church administration, scholarship, schools, and universities after it ceased to be most people's native speech.
One script can be adapted to many languages without making those languages identical.
contested_or_missing: The exact time and place of Greek alphabet adaptation remain debated.
These sources do not by themselves explain every later imperial, colonial, educational, or digital expansion of Latin script.
task_lessons: Latin-script familiarity is model-history evidence, not script superiority.
Do not treat alphabetic writing as a progress endpoint.

historical_witnesses.ecology: Arabic, Persian, and Islamicate scholarly and administrative networks
historical_witnesses.period: Early Islamic centuries through transregional Persianate and modern digital use
places: Central and South Asian Persianate networks
established: Arabic script serves several unrelated languages.
Persian adapted Arabic script and substantial learned vocabulary while retaining Iranian genealogy.
Greek-to-Syriac and Greek-or-Syriac-to-Arabic learning and translation networks operated across distinct communities and institutional settings.
A modern translation-studies account describes medieval Arabic translation as meaning-remaking rather than simple lexical equivalence.
contested_or_missing: Written sources incompletely reveal spoken borrowing by period and class.
No loanword percentage establishes language identity or value.
task_lessons: Same script does not mean same morphology or language.
Retain source terms, diacritics policy, directionality, and translator choices.

historical_witnesses.ecology: Swahili contact and African script-plurality ecology
historical_witnesses.period: Indian Ocean contact traditions through colonial standardization and modern community scripts
places: East African coast and interior networks
language_varieties: Languages using Ethiopic, Vai, Bamum, N'Ko, Adlam, and other scripts
established: Kiswahili is a Bantu language developed on the East African coast.
Swahili settlements and later language spread participated in African, Indian Ocean, educational, religious, political, and urban networks.
Arabic-script Swahili has a documented manuscript history and was later officially forbidden or marginalized in named colonial settings.
African writing includes many distinct and deliberate community innovations.
contested_or_missing: Colonial catalogues and script policy create archival discontinuities.
No one standard variety represents all Swahili communities.
task_lessons: Search historical scripts and variant orthographies.
Absence from a Latin corpus is not absence of history or reasoning.

historical_witnesses.ecology: Maya logosyllabic, colonial alphabetic, and living-language ecology
historical_witnesses.period: Pre-Hispanic Maya writing through colonial rupture, alphabetic adaptation, decipherment, and revival
established: Maya writing was fully logosyllabic.
Maya political and linguistic life was plural.
Colonial violence radically selected the surviving corpus while alphabetic Indigenous writing continued.
contested_or_missing: Only a tiny share of pre-Hispanic books survives.
Undeciphered and unencoded signs remain technical and scholarly unknowns rather than cultural absence.
task_lessons: Keep source image, sign reading, transcription, translation, and interpretation separate.
Encoding status never measures vitality or worth.

language_profiles.family_note: Semitic language profile scoped to formal written source terminology; regional spoken Arabic varieties are not collapsed into it.
language_profiles.period_and_region: Source-dependent formal Arabic across Islamicate scholarly networks; exact source period must be carried by each artifact.
language_profiles.variety: Formal written Arabic; source-specific classical or modern register must be declared later.

scripts.name: Arabic
layout_notes: Short-vowel marking is source- and register-dependent.
Bidirectional isolation is required when embedded in left-to-right prose.

morphology_notes: Root-pattern morphology and inflection make word-level substitution unsafe.
Clitics can attach to orthographic words.
syntax_notes: Word order and agreement depend on variety, genre, and information structure.
discourse_notes: Formal, scriptural, technical, and regional registers must not be conflated.
historical_roles: Translation and administration in named periods

language_profiles.family_note: Iranian Indo-European language profile; shared Arabic-derived script and borrowed vocabulary do not make Persian Semitic or Arabic.
language_profiles.period_and_region: New Persian sources across Iranian, Central Asian, and South Asian networks; exact source period and variety remain artifact-local.
language_profiles.variety: Source-dependent literary or formal New Persian.

scripts.name: Perso-Arabic
layout_notes: Persian extends Arabic script for Persian phonemes.
Some visually related Arabic and Persian code points require exact source retention.
Bidirectional isolation is required inside left-to-right prose.

morphology_notes: Persian morphology and syntax remain distinct from Arabic despite learned borrowing.
Compounding and enclitic behaviour require source-aware segmentation.
syntax_notes: Modifier and complement patterns cannot be inferred from the shared script.
discourse_notes: Loan vocabulary varies by period, genre, and formality.

language_profiles.family_note: Germanic Indo-European language profile used only because the planned audience requested English; current model and platform prevalence is not inherent superiority.
language_profiles.period_and_region: Contemporary international written English for this planned public brief.
language_profiles.variety: Plain international English with source terms retained.

scripts.name: Latin
layout_notes: Romanization is a separate artifact from Arabic- or Persian-script text.

morphology_notes: Analytic tendencies do not make English a neutral formal interlingua.
syntax_notes: English clause order can force choices not explicit in a source expression.
discourse_notes: Plain language can still erase honorific, evidential, rhetorical, or genre distinctions unless recorded.
historical_roles: Requested audience interface in this fixture
Current high-resource model language under many undisclosed training mixtures

shape.label: Inscription, glyph, direction, and medium
shape.definition: Material and graphic organization including stroke, wedge, joining, block, direction, line, page, and medium.

shape.label: Unicode, normalization, and grapheme shape
shape.definition: Exact code-point sequences, canonical or compatibility normalization, combining sequences, and declared grapheme segmentation.

shape.label: Morphological shape
shape.definition: Roots, patterns, stems, affixes, clitics, compounds, agreement, sandhi, and language-specific word boundaries.

shape.label: Syntactic and relational shape
shape.definition: Dependency, constituency, argument structure, information structure, and permitted order in a named variety and register.

shape.label: Discourse, genre, and register shape
shape.definition: Audience, genre, honorifics, quotation, evidential stance, formality, and institutional use.

shape.label: Tokenizer sequence shape
shape.definition: The exact sequence produced by one named tokenizer revision from exact input bytes or Unicode text.

shape.label: Model representation geometry
shape.definition: A model-, layer-, position-, prompt-, tokenizer-, and estimator-specific relation among activations.

weight.label: Historical and institutional weight
weight.definition: Scoped relations in which named institutions teach, require, archive, fund, suppress, or publish a variety or script in a period and domain.

weight.label: Corpus prevalence weight
weight.definition: A language or variety's measured share of one named training or evaluation corpus.

weight.label: Token and context cost weight
weight.definition: Tokens, bytes, or retained graphemes consumed by aligned content under one exact tokenizer revision and denominator.

weight.label: Task-local evidence weight
weight.definition: Results from a named benchmark or competent review under a fixed model, prompt, language, date, and task.

weight.label: Parameter or runtime activation weight
weight.definition: Learned numerical parameters or runtime activation and attention values in one named model and intervention context.

observations.statement: Cuneiform, Han characters, Brahmi descendants, Arabic script, and Latin script crossed language boundaries; script identity therefore does not determine language genealogy or grammar.
observations.scope: The cited historical ecologies and source descriptions only.
limitations: Each transfer involved different mechanisms, actors, and losses.
The cases do not exhaust world writing systems.

observations.statement: One language can occupy several scripts, media, and social registers while a prestigious script or register can persist after speech and grammar change.
observations.scope: Especially the Egyptian, Latin, Sanskrit–Prakrit, Literary Chinese, and Arabic–Persian evidence reviewed here.
limitations: Register labels are analytic summaries and may not match historical participants' categories.

observations.statement: Durable, official, sacred, and elite records are often overrepresented, while ordinary, oral, perishable, suppressed, and community-restricted expression is often underrepresented.
observations.scope: A cross-case archival warning supported by the reviewed corpora and colonial rupture cases.
limitations: The direction and degree of selection must be established separately for each corpus.
does_not_establish: That every surviving record is elite
That missing expression did not exist

observations.statement: Token count, price, and effective context coverage can vary substantially across aligned languages under a particular commercial tokenizer and model.
observations.scope: The 22-language systems studied by Ahia and colleagues in 2023.
limitations: Tokenizers, models, prices, and evaluation quality change.
Aligned meaning and aligned string length are not identical.

observations.statement: When evaluation expands beyond frequently benchmarked languages, high- and low-resource performance gaps remain visible even on a simple task.
observations.scope: SIB-200 topic classification across 205 languages and dialects.
limitations: One translated topic-classification benchmark does not measure every real-world task.

observations.statement: Adding multilingual data can help or interfere depending on resource level, language similarity, dataset size, and model capacity.
observations.scope: More than 10,000 controlled language models up to 45 million parameters across more than 250 languages.
limitations: Small-model pretraining results do not transfer automatically to large instruction-tuned systems.

observations.statement: XLM-R exhibited both shared mean-centred subspace structure and language-sensitive representation means, some with causal effects on output language.
observations.scope: XLM-R, the tested 88 languages, layers, stimuli, estimators, and interventions.
limitations: Shared axes are not a language-neutral ontology.
Other models and tasks may organize representations differently.

observations.statement: Ordinary attention weights can diverge from other feature-importance measures, and different attention distributions can preserve the same output.
observations.scope: Selected NLP tasks and attention architectures in Jain and Wallace 2019.
limitations: This does not show that every attention intervention is causally irrelevant.
does_not_establish: That one token's weight equals semantic importance

observations.statement: Translation to English can help some English-centric model tasks but is not universally optimal; native-language prompting can better preserve culture-related nuance in tested settings.
observations.scope: The models, languages, real-world queries, and NLP tasks studied by Liu and colleagues in 2025.
limitations: Native-language advantage is not universal and must be retested per task and model.
does_not_establish: English is the best reasoning language

observations.statement: General multilingual capability did not reliably entail code-switching understanding or generation across the tested tasks, pairs, models, and prompts.
observations.scope: The 2023 code-switching and Southeast Asian code-mixed studies cited here.
limitations: Models and prompting have changed since 2023.
Human code-switching practices are community- and context-specific.

invariants.statement: Exact source bytes or an exact source locator remain distinct from every normalized, transliterated, translated, or interpreted artifact.
A shared script never establishes shared language genealogy, grammar, community, religion, polity, or identity.
invariants.scope: All language assignments, historical claims, and translations.

invariants.statement: Names, dates, numbers, units, and cited locators remain source-linked and are checked before completion.
invariants.scope: Draft, translation, review, and fused output.

invariants.statement: Negation, modality, uncertainty, quotation, and evidence posture are not strengthened or dropped silently.
invariants.scope: Every translation, summary, and fusion edge.

invariants.statement: Material Arabic and Persian terms remain visible beside bounded transliteration and gloss rather than being replaced by one English token.
invariants.scope: Terminology table, draft, review, and final output.

invariants.statement: A claim about one period, region, genre, or register is not generalized to a timeless whole language or civilisation.
invariants.scope: Historical source extraction and public drafting.

invariants.statement: Quoted, transcribed, normalized, translated, inferred, and agent-drafted content keep distinct provenance labels.
A sourced material disagreement or alternative is retained until a named evidence process resolves it; majority output cannot erase it.
Missing evidence, untested model behaviour, unencoded signs, and inaccessible sources remain unknown or not represented rather than becoming negative facts.
Visibility or technical accessibility does not override community access conditions, refusal, restricted knowledge, or the need for competent review.
invariants.scope: Source selection, artifact handling, and publication decisions.

invariants.statement: Tasks exchange attributed public or safely redacted artifacts, never hidden chain-of-thought or private activations.
invariants.scope: Every task dependency and fusion input.

run_cards.executor_label: Unbound Unicode and tokenizer audit role

tests.condition: The closed record, references, artifact production, assignments, dependency graph, transformations, and fixed non-grants validate.
limitations: Structural validity does not assess the truth of prose or source destinations.

tests.condition: Every normalized, transliterated, translated, or fused form retains an exact source locator or byte-bound witness without overwrite.
limitations: A retained hash proves byte identity only when the referenced bytes are actually available and verified.

tests.condition: Declared canonical normalization views preserve canonical comparison while exact source bytes remain recoverable.
limitations: Canonical equivalence is not glyph, layout, pronunciation, or semantic equivalence.

tests.condition: Extended grapheme clusters and script-tailored exceptions are not split, truncated, or silently reordered in the tested renderer.
limitations: Unicode default grapheme clusters approximate rather than exhaust user-perceived characters.

tests.condition: Arabic- and Persian-script spans render in intended order with punctuation, numbers, identifiers, and embeddings isolated under named clients.
limitations: One renderer result cannot establish all client behaviour.

tests.condition: Names, dates, numbers, units, negation, modality, uncertainty, and quotation status match the named source artifacts under a visible comparison.
limitations: Passing listed invariants does not prove complete translation fidelity.

tests.condition: Every material term keeps source form, provenance, transliteration where used, literal and idiomatic gloss distinction, register, ambiguity, and prohibited conflations.
limitations: Terminology review remains period-, domain-, and source-bound.

tests.condition: Literal, idiomatic, declined, and alternative mappings remain distinct and the loss vector is reviewed rather than collapsed to one score.
limitations: A contrastive artifact does not itself establish which mapping an audience should choose.

tests.condition: For one exact model and tokenizer revision, report tokens, Unicode graphemes, code points, UTF-8 bytes, and retained aligned coverage without assigning language value.
limitations: Token count is model-specific and does not measure semantic retention alone.

tests.condition: Each proposed language-task role is evaluated on this fixture under exact model, tokenizer, prompt, date, criteria, and limitations before capability language is used.
limitations: One fixture cannot establish general language competence or permanent expertise.

tests.condition: A competent, properly scoped reviewer can accept, challenge, decline, or leave unknown without their identity being inferred or their silence treated as consent.
limitations: Native-speaker status is neither automatically inferable nor sufficient for every historical or technical domain.

tests.condition: Shared model, prompt, source, translator, reviewer, and tool dependencies are declared before agreement affects confidence.
limitations: Declared independence remains a claim until operationally verified.

tests.condition: Every material sourced alternative remains linked in the fused artifact unless a named evidence process resolves or withdraws it.
limitations: Retention does not imply equal evidential support for every position.

unknowns.question: Which exact model, tokenizer, prompt, adapter, and reviewer should execute each role?
unknowns.why_unknown: No executor has been selected or evaluated and the protocol forbids choosing from historical prestige or apparent multilingual fluency.
unknowns.stop_condition: Do not claim capability or execute the graph while roles remain unbound.

unknowns.question: Which Arabic and Persian terms are material to the final brief and which mappings should be declined?
unknowns.why_unknown: No source extraction or terminology review has run.
unknowns.stop_condition: Do not publish a source-language claim without its source form and provenance.

unknowns.question: What token, grapheme, byte, and retained-context differences arise under the future selected tokenizer?
unknowns.why_unknown: No model or tokenizer revision is bound and no text artifact exists.
unknowns.stop_condition: Do not generalize any token-cost observation to this weave before measurement.

unknowns.question: Which reviewers have the source, historical, technical, and community competence required for the final stakes?
unknowns.why_unknown: No reviewer, role scope, independence claim, or access condition has been established.
unknowns.stop_condition: Do not upgrade the weave beyond planned or use it for high-stakes decisions without competent review.

unknowns.question: Do any selected source materials carry community access, attribution, or restricted-knowledge conditions beyond public visibility?
unknowns.why_unknown: URL accessibility and schema validity do not establish community consent or governance conditions.
unknowns.stop_condition: Stop when access or community authority is unresolved for a requested use.

repair.correction_route: Create a new version linked to this weave, name every affected artifact and task, carry material disagreements and unknowns, rerun relevant tests, and state any privacy or safety removal.
